intro: Eugen d’Albert, a pupil of Liszt, plays Chopin’s Étude in G♭ major, Op. 25 No. 9, the Butterfly, in an Odeon recording made in 1912–13. The étude is written in short slurs and detached octaves.

sections.label: A · Short slurs and detached octaves
sections.mNote: The right hand alternates slurred pairs with detached notes.

sections.label: B · octaves across the keyboard
sections.mNote: The four-note figure changes key and climbs.

sections.label: C · The short figure returns
sections.mNote: Right-hand octaves continue above the left hand’s leaps

sections.label: D · The last piano chords fade
sections.mNote: The study closes and the piano falls silent

cues.title: Right-hand figure and left-hand leaps
cues.text: The right hand’s four-note groups mix short slurs with detached notes and octaves. The left hand leaps between bass notes and chords. Chopin keeps this figure throughout the étude, moving it to other keys and registers.
cues.evidence: The recurring motif, key changes and staccato octaves: Mieczysław Tomaszewski, https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/263. Left-hand leaps and right-hand groups: Fred Yu, https://www.ourchopin.com/analysis/etude25.html.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Training and operas
cues.text: D’Albert was born in Glasgow in 1864, far from the German concert halls that later made his name. He studied in London with teachers including Arthur Sullivan, then went to Liszt. Alongside his career at the piano he wrote operas; Tiefland reached the stage in 1903.
cues.evidence: Baker’s Biographical Dictionary of Musicians: Glasgow birth, London training with Sullivan, study with Liszt and the 15 November 1903 Prague premiere of Tiefland. https://www.encyclopedia.com/arts/dictionaries-thesauruses-pictures-and-press-releases/dalbert-eugen-actually-eugene-francischarles

cues.title: Odeon disc 76563
cues.text: Odeon issued Butterfly with Chopin’s F-minor étude, Op. 25 No. 2, under catalogue number 76563. Both pieces share one recording matrix. This short G♭-major study is the second half of the original disc side.
cues.evidence: Printed Symposium 1146 track list gives both études the same Odeon catalogue number 76563 and matrix xxB 5731, dated 1912/3. https://archive.org/download/02-eugen-d-albert-syposium-1146/D%27Albert%20tracks.jpg. The Archive filename specifies March 1913; the printed discography gives only the year range.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
